item.title: Zuiryuji Temple: A National Treasure Zen Complex in Takaoka — Guide
item.description: Zuiryuji Temple was built in the mid-17th century by Maeda Toshitsune, second lord of the powerful Kaga domain, to honour his father and predecessor, and today stands as one of the finest surviving examples of early Edo-period Zen temple architecture in Japan. Its main hall, sanmon gate and dharma hall are all designated National Treasures, connected by covered corridors in a symmetrical layout characteristic of formal Zen temple design, offering visitors a rare chance to walk through a complete, historically intact temple complex.

item.title: Osaki Hachimangu: Sendai's National Treasure Shrine — Guide
item.description: Built by Date Masamune in 1607, Osaki Hachimangu is one of Japan’s most elegant shrine buildings — a National Treasure clad in gold lacquer and vivid black urushi lacquerwork, blending Momoyama-period opulence with subdued Zen restraint. The long approach through an ancient cedar grove creates a quiet transition from the modern city outside. Every January the shrine hosts the Dontosai festival, and each November families bring children for Shichi-Go-San blessing ceremonies.

item.title: Shiramizu Amidado: A Heian-Era National Treasure Temple — Guide
item.description: Shiramizu Amidado, built in 1160 by the widow of a regional lord to pray for her late husband’s soul, is a National Treasure and one of only a handful of surviving Heian-period Pure Land Buddhist temple gardens in Japan. The hall sits on an island in a lotus pond, meant to evoke the Buddhist paradise of the Pure Land, with the wooden structure and its seated Amida Buddha reflected serenely in the water — a rare, intact glimpse of 12th-century religious architecture.
